class.name: CameraAttributes
class.description: Controls camera-specific attributes such as depth of field and exposure override. When used in a [WorldEnvironment] it provides default settings for exposure, auto-exposure, and depth of field that will be used by all cameras without their own [CameraAttributes], including the editor camera. When used in a [Camera3D] it will override any [CameraAttributes] set in the [WorldEnvironment]. When used in [VoxelGI] or [LightmapGI], only the exposure settings will be used. See also [Environment] for general 3D environment settings. This is a pure virtual class that is inherited by [CameraAttributesPhysical] and [CameraAttributesPractical].

members.member: If [code]true[/code], enables the tonemapping auto exposure mode of the scene renderer. If [code]true[/code], the renderer will automatically determine the exposure setting to adapt to the scene's illumination and the observed light. [b]Note:[/b] Auto-exposure is only supported in the Forward+ rendering method, not Mobile or Compatibility.
The scale of the auto exposure effect. Affects the intensity of auto exposure.
The speed of the auto exposure effect. Affects the time needed for the camera to perform auto exposure.

How far red and blue fringes spread at the frame's corners, as a percentage of the distance from the centre. The lens images red slightly larger and blue slightly smaller than green, so the fringes grow from nothing at the centre; each colour is spread over a short spectrum rather than shifted as a whole. [code]0.25[/code] spreads red and blue by about 3 pixels in the corners at 1080p.
If [code]true[/code], splits red and blue towards the frame's edges, as a cheap lens does (lateral chromatic aberration). [b]Note:[/b] Only supported in the Forward+ rendering method.
Multiplier for the exposure amount. A higher value results in a brighter image.

Sensitivity of camera sensors, measured in ISO. A higher sensitivity results in a brighter image. If [member auto_exposure_enabled] is [code]true[/code], this can be used as a method of exposure compensation, doubling the value will increase the exposure value (measured in EV100) by 1 stop. [b]Note:[/b] Only available when [member ProjectSettings.rendering/lights_and_shadows/use_physical_light_units] is enabled.

Strength of the grain. At [code]1.0[/code], grain moves the tones it affects most up and down by up to 10% of full brightness. Grain is strongest in the darker midtones (around a quarter of full brightness) and weaker in deep shadows and highlights, as on film.
If [code]true[/code], adds monochrome film grain that changes every frame. It is applied after tonemapping, to the picture as displayed. [b]Note:[/b] Only supported in the Forward+ rendering method.
Size of a grain, in pixels at 1080p; it scales with the resolution, so the grain looks the same at any resolution.

How long the shutter stays open, as a fraction of the time between two frames: [code]0.5[/code] blurs each moving pixel over half of its motion during a frame (a 180 degree shutter), [code]1.0[/code] over all of it. Higher values give longer streaks. If [member motion_blur_target_fps] is above [code]0[/code], the frame time is that frame rate's instead of the real one.

If [code]true[/code], blurs the picture along the motion of the camera and of moving objects, using the same motion vectors as temporal antialiasing. Objects with [member GeometryInstance3D.exclude_from_motion_blur] are neither blurred nor smeared over their surroundings (for first-person weapons and the player's vehicle). Streaks are limited to about 4% of the viewport's height on either side of a pixel. Transparent objects are blurred with what is behind them. [b]Note:[/b] Motion blur is only supported in the Forward+ rendering method, not Mobile or Compatibility.

If above [code]0[/code], the blur is as long as it would be at this frame rate, whatever the real frame rate is, so that a game looks the same at 60 and at 144 FPS. If [code]0[/code], the blur follows the real time between frames: faster frame rates blur less.

If [code]true[/code], darkens the picture towards its corners, as a lens does. It is applied before tonemapping, so bright lights in the corners still clip. [b]Note:[/b] Only supported in the Forward+ rendering method.
How dark the corners get: [code]0.5[/code] halves the light in the corners, [code]1.0[/code] makes them black.
Where the darkening starts, as a share of the way from the centre to the corners. Inside it the picture is untouched.
